answers.text:
Transfer entropy is a directional information-theoretic measure that captures how much knowing a source neuron's past activity reduces uncertainty about a target neuron's future activity, beyond what the target's own past already tells you. The article defines it more formally a few sentences later: transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on the target's own past.

What makes it different from plain mutual information (its neighbor in this same sentence) is the built-in sense of direction and time. Mutual information just asks whether two neurons' activities are statistically dependent, with no notion of "before" and "after." Transfer entropy, by contrast, is explicitly framed as a flow from one neuron to another: TE(X → Y) is read as the transfer entropy from X's past to Y's future, and it quantifies how much the past of the source variable reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target's own past. The article underscores this distinction a bit further on by noting that whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity — meaning it's used to infer something closer to actual information propagation between neurons, not just correlation.

This matters for the rest of the review because transfer entropy becomes the workhorse for building the directed "effective networks" from spike recordings that the authors later feed into partial information decomposition (PID) — the framework the paper is really building toward. It's introduced here, alongside mutual information, as one of the two basic tools for tracking information movement in a circuit before the paper turns to the more complex question of how neurons actually process (rather than merely relay) that information.

answers.asked: Information-theoretic tools such as mutual information [10] and transfer entropy [11] are well suited to this purpose.
answers.text:
This sentence introduces the two main tools the article uses to track information flow between neurons, before it defines either one in detail — the actual definitions come in the very next block, spya-f6sbgx and spya-p4pyuy.

Mutual information measures the statistical dependence between two neurons' activity: how much our ability to correctly infer the state of X changes depending on whether we account for shared dependencies with Y, thought of as a kind of nonlinear correlation. Crucially, the article notes it does not quantify information transfer, since it is an undirected measure with no notion of time-directed "flow".

Transfer entropy fixes that gap: it asks how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on the target's own past. The article distinguishes the two by likening mutual information to functional connectivity and transfer entropy to effective connectivity — transfer entropy provides a measure of information propagation, whereas mutual information just captures co-variation without direction.

So this sentence is a signpost: it names the pair of classical tools (undirected correlation vs. directed flow) that the article will use to establish *that* information moves through a circuit — setting up the next section's argument that these tools, however, still can't capture information *processing* (how sources combine or interact), which is why the paper goes on to introduce partial information decomposition.

answers.asked: What does "transfer entropy" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
Transfer entropy is defined in the article as a measure of how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, once you've already conditioned on that second neuron's own past (its autocorrelation) [spya-p4pyuy]. The article gives it formally: Transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron (e.g., Xp) accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron (e.g., Yt+1), conditioned on Y's own past (Yp), and glosses TE(X→Y) as being read as the transfer entropy from X's past to Y's future. The article distinguishes it explicitly from mutual information: Whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity, so that transfer entropy provides a measure of information propagation rather than just an undirected statistical association.

Why it matters to the argument: the whole empirical program in the piece is built on transfer entropy as the tool for turning raw spike recordings into a directed effective network in the first place, before partial information decomposition (PID) is even applied. The authors describe rendering 512-channel multielectrode arrays to record hundreds of individual neurons in vitro from organotypic cultures derived from mouse cortical slices... into an effective network, capturing the microcircuit dynamics using transfer entropy. Only once that TE-based network of source→target links exists can they identify the two-source, one-target "triads" that PID decomposes into redundant, unique, and synergistic information [spya-sw5ukx]. TE also becomes a variable in its own right in the results: the article reports that synergy varies systematically as a function of the amount of information propagation—the transfer entropy from sources to a target—across triads, finding a strong correlation and that the amount of synergy observed in a given triad was reliably about a quarter of the transfer entropy for that triad. So transfer entropy does double duty in the argument: it is the method for building the networks that PID is applied to, and it is one of the key quantities whose relationship to synergy the empirical sections are trying to characterize (feedforward strength, rich-club structure, timescale effects, etc.).

One caveat the article itself flags: because these networks were built with *bivariate* transfer entropy, it has been shown that bivariate analyses overestimate the significance of bivariate edges, which the authors list as a limitation of the in vitro work [spya-j4cy9j].

Synergistic information is one of the three basic "modes" the paper's framework — partial information decomposition (PID) — sorts information into, alongside redundant and unique. It refers specifically to information about a target (say, a neuron's future firing) that only becomes available when you look at multiple sources *together*, and that vanishes if you look at any one source on its own.

The abstract flags this as the mode the authors care about most: "We focus particularly on the synergistic mode, which quantifies the 'higher-order' information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source." The intuition, spelled out later in the article, is that if you sum up how much each input neuron individually tells you about the target, that sum can actually be *less* than what you learn from knowing all the inputs jointly — the leftover, non-additive information is the synergy, and it's treated as a signature of genuine "computation" or integration happening at the target, rather than just passive relay of signals from upstream neurons. This is why the abstract later notes "synergistic dynamics are ubiquitous in neural circuitry and show reliable structure–function relationships, emerging disproportionately in neuronal rich clubs, downstream of recurrent connectivity, and in the convergence of correlated activity."

At this point in the abstract, the term is just being introduced as a label; the article hasn't yet given the formal definition — that comes later, in the section on PID (around the two-parent-neuron example), where synergy is defined precisely as the gap between the joint mutual information from all sources together and the sum of what each source discloses alone.

answers.asked: PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources.
answers.text:
This is naming the three "modes" that partial information decomposition (PID) sorts information into — the framework the abstract is flagging as the paper's main tool, before the rest of the article unpacks it in detail (Section 4).

The setup is a target neuron receiving input from two or more source neurons. PID asks: how much does knowing the sources' activity reduce our uncertainty about the target's future firing, and how is that total information built up out of contributions from the sources? The three modes are the possible ways a piece of information can relate to the sources considered individually versus jointly. As the article later explains with the two-parent case: "Red(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that could be learned by observing X₁ or X₂, Unq(Xᵢ;Y) is the information about Y that could only be learned by observing Xᵢ, and Syn(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that can only be learned by observing the joint states of X₁ and X₂ together."

So redundant information is duplicated across sources (either one alone tells you the same thing); unique information is exclusive to one particular source; and synergistic information only shows up when you look at the sources' joint pattern — neither one alone reveals it. The article stresses that this last category is the interesting one for "processing," since it captures genuine integration rather than mere summation: "if the whole is less than the sum of its parts, then there must be redundant information about Y instantiated multiple times over the parent neurons that is 'double counted' when summing the marginals." The abstract itself signals this emphasis, noting the review focuses on synergy as "the 'higher-order' information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source."

The sentence you selected is essentially a one-line preview of a whole apparatus (mutual information equations, the "partial information lattice," redundancy functions) that the paper builds out later — the words "redundant," "unique," and "synergistic" are technical terms of art specific to this framework, not loose synonyms, and they recur as load-bearing vocabulary throughout the rest of the review.

answers.asked: What does "synergistic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Synergistic" information is the piece of the joint mutual information that neither source neuron discloses on its own — the part of what a target neuron "knows" about its inputs that only shows up when you look at the sources *together*. The article defines it formally: if the joint mutual information from both parent neurons (the "whole") is greater than the sum of what each parent tells you individually (the "parts"), then there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any individual parent. In this case, the system exhibits synergistic dynamics, and the target neuron can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating "computation" on all of its inputs considered jointly [spya-e94ury]. Figure 1's description puts it geometrically: the joint state of X1 and X2 can account for the activity of Y to some degree. This information is not accounted for by either source independently and is the synergistic information that X1 and X2 carry about Y [spya-pjdgu6]. It sits alongside redundant information (disclosed by either source alone) and unique information (disclosed only by one particular source) in the partial information decomposition [spya-h5jzvm].

Why it matters to the argument: the whole point of the paper is that synergy is the signature of genuine information *processing*, as opposed to mere information *transfer*. The authors say plainly that transfer entropy tracks flow but is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information "interact" and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources [spya-s0db2g] — synergy is what fills that gap, capturing the "higher-order" combination effect that a single-source measure can't see. The empirical sections then use synergy as their main dependent variable: it is found to be denser in neuronal rich clubs [spya-fud8q3], to rise with recurrent connectivity [spya-sd9fzd], to peak at intermediate correlation between source neurons [spya-ybmve2], and to shift with behavioral task demands in primates [spya-t8fayf]. The summary makes the stakes explicit: The existence of synergy in empirical data shows us that neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total (as would be expected from a basic threshold model or complex contagion model), but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli [spya-sp50v3]. So synergy is doing the argumentative work of showing that neurons are pattern-detectors, not simple summers — that's the empirical payoff the whole review is built around.
